title: From one token, see the whole computer
deck: You type a sentence into the chat box. What happens inside your computer? First, draw the whole map.
prereq: None. Having used a chat AI such as ChatGPT is enough.
goals: Explain what the model, the inference engine and the app are each responsible for
Draw the path a sentence takes from input to output
Tell whether a number is a code fact, an upstream report or an estimate

quiz.text: The README says "each word it writes needs only 10 experts". According to the source code, how many expert picks does generating one token take in total?
quiz.why: 10 is the number picked in each layer. 48 layers each pick 10, for 480 in total; 24,576 is the total number of experts, not the number used each time.

quiz.text: A browser experiment shows "120 token/s". What is this number?
choices: Strata's measured speed on your graphics card
An estimate computed from teaching assumptions
A speed any computer can reach
quiz.why: The browser experiment does not run the real model and does not time anything on your hardware. It is a teaching estimate and must not be called a measurement.

quiz.text: A source comment says "no cache here yet". What should you do next?
choices: Conclude right away that the feature does not exist
Trace the current calling code and the default configuration
Delete that code
quiz.why: Comments can be stuck at an old stage of development. Only the current call chain, default configuration and tests let you draw a conclusion.

problem: A friend says: "Strata runs a 125-billion-parameter model on a 12 GB graphics card, so it must compress the model to under 12 GB." What is wrong with this sentence? Use this chapter to rewrite it as an accurate one.
answer: Quantization does compress the model: in the standard format each parameter takes about 2.25 bits. But all the experts together still take about 34 GB, far more than 12 GB. Strata relies on tiered storage: the parts every token needs and the most used experts sit in VRAM, all the experts sit in RAM, and experts not on the GPU are mostly computed by the CPU right there in RAM. An accurate version: Strata spreads the model across the GPU, RAM and SSD, and keeps only the most used parts on the GPU.

title: Tokens, conditional probability and sampling
deck: The model never just says the next word: it first produces a probability table, then rolls the dice.
prereq: Chapter 1. Being able to multiply and divide decimals, and having seen powers of e, is enough.
goals: Use the chain rule to explain how a model generates text one token at a time
Work out softmax by hand, and explain what temperature and "subtracting the max" each do
Tell a distribution apart from a draw, and explain why the seed and the order of the sampling chain affect the result

quiz.text: You send the model the same sentence, changing only the role tags in the chat template. Is the model still reading the same question?
choices: Yes, the words you typed did not change
No, the template is input too, so the ID sequence changed
It depends on the temperature
quiz.why: The template wraps around your words, and everything is cut into IDs together. Change the tags and the ID sequence changes; to the model, it is a different question.

quiz.text: If you subtract the same number (say, the maximum) from every score, what happens to the probabilities softmax computes?
choices: Nothing changes, they just become less likely to overflow
They all get smaller
The ranking gets shuffled
quiz.why: e^(z−m) = e^z ÷ e^m, so the numerator and denominator are divided by the same number and the ratio stays the same. After subtracting the max, the largest term is e^0 = 1, so nothing overflows.

quiz.text: With temperature 0 and a fixed seed, will asking the same question twice always give a word-for-word identical answer?
choices: Always identical
Not necessarily: a tiny floating-point rounding difference can swap a token
Always different
quiz.why: Temperature 0 only guarantees picking the top score at every step. Different kernels sum in different orders, so the last digits of the scores can differ, and when candidates score almost the same, a token can be swapped. Strata's docs record such a case: you have to turn off several settings to repeat byte for byte.

problem: Scores z = [2, 1, 0], temperature T = 1. ① Compute the three probabilities and the cumulative probabilities. ② Which entry do the random numbers u = 0.5 and u = 0.95 each pick? ③ Why can you not judge whether two runs had the same scores just by comparing their final text?
answer: ① Subtract the maximum 2 to get [0, −1, −2]; the exponentials are about [1, 0.3679, 0.1353], the sum is 1.5032, the probabilities are about [0.6652, 0.2447, 0.0900], and the cumulative values are [0.6652, 0.9100, 1]. ② u = 0.5 is below 0.6652, so it picks the first entry; u = 0.95 falls in [0.9100, 1), so it picks the third. ③ Different scores can still pick the same token, so the same text does not mean the same scores; and scores that differ only slightly can swap a token at some step, after which the whole rest of the text forks. You should compare the probability tables directly, under the same history.

title: A tensor is memory with coordinates
deck: Linear algebra answers "what to compute"; memory layout answers "which cell to fetch the number from".
prereq: Chapter 1. Knowing what a vector and a table are is enough.
goals: Multiply a matrix by a vector by hand, and explain the difference between GEMV and GEMM
Use the shape and strides to compute the memory address of any element
Explain why the layout belongs in the interface and why shapes are checked at load time

quiz.text: W has 2 rows and 3 columns, and x has 3 numbers. How many numbers are in y = Wx, and how many multiply-adds does it take?
choices: 3 numbers, 6 multiply-adds
2 numbers, 6 multiply-adds
2 numbers, 5 multiply-adds
quiz.why: W has 2 rows, so you take 2 dot products and get 2 numbers; each dot product has 3 multiply-adds, for 2 × 3 = 6 in total.

quiz.text: Two tensors have exactly the same shape. Can you use one's memory directly as the other?
choices: Yes, the same shape is enough
Not necessarily: the strides (layout) and the meaning of the data may differ
Yes, as long as both are float
quiz.why: The shape only says which coordinates exist; the strides decide which cell each coordinate maps to. Strata's GDN state has the same shape in the reference implementation and in the kernel, but a different layout.

quiz.text: A three-dimensional array of shape (2, 3, 2) is stored in row-major order. What is the address of element (1, 2, 0)?
quiz.why: The strides are (6, 2, 1), so the address = 1×6 + 2×2 + 0×1 = 10. The (i, j, h) layout gives 8, which is just as valid; that is exactly why using the wrong layout raises no error.

problem: You are writing the interface notes for an "expert compute" function. It takes a float* input and hands back a float* output. Write down at least five contracts that must be stated, and point out which of them the C++ type float* itself cannot express.
answer: At least: ① the shape (2560 numbers in, 2560 numbers out); ② the layout or strides (contiguous or not, which axis is fastest); ③ whether the input is already normalized; ④ whether the output has already been multiplied by the routing weight (Strata says the expert pool does not multiply; it happens only once, when combining); ⑤ who owns the buffer, how long it can be used, and whether its address is reused (Strata uses the same block of pinned memory for every layer's input: the address stays the same while the content changes). You should also state whether the pointer points to CPU memory or VRAM. float* only says "points to floating-point numbers"; it expresses none of the above, not even the length, so only interface notes, semantic types and tests can guard them.

title: Quantization: fewer bits, not less error
deck: Store fewer bits and get a smaller model; the price is error, and the error has to be measured.
prereq: Chapter 3. Knowing how to round and what binary is, is enough.
goals: Explain where FP32, FP16 and BF16 spend their bits, and how they trade range against precision
Quantize one symmetric block by hand: the scale, the codes, the restored values and the error
Work out the real bit width of a quantization format, and explain why Strata's experts take 2.25 bits

quiz.text: 32 four-bit codes plus one 16-bit scale. How many bits does each weight really take on average?
choices: 4 bits
4.5 bits
16 bits
quiz.why: (32 × 4 + 16) ÷ 32 = 4.5. The scale takes space too, so the nominal bit width is not the real bit width.

quiz.text: A number is 70000. What happens if you store it in FP16 and in BF16?
choices: Both can store it, and accurately
FP16 overflows to infinity; BF16 can store it, but not very accurately
Both overflow
quiz.why: FP16 has only 5 exponent bits, so its maximum is 65504. BF16 has 8 exponent bits and the same range as FP32, but only 7 mantissa bits, so 70000 is stored as 70144.

quiz.text: A group of 16 small weights also contains one very large outlier, and they share one scale for 4-bit quantization. What happens?
choices: Nothing much; only the outlier itself has some error
The scale is stretched, and many small weights are rounded to 0
Every weight's error becomes 0
quiz.why: The scale is set by the number with the largest absolute value in the block. The outlier makes the marks coarse, and the small numbers fall onto level 0. Smaller blocks reduce the damage, at the cost of storing more scales.

problem: Someone says: "Strata's 4-bit KV cache just shrinks the chat history by half, with no loss of quality at all." What kind of evidence would this claim need? Propose two tests you could actually run, and say what result the upstream docs report.
answer: Quantization changes the values of K and V, and in a long conversation attention reads them again and again, so errors may build up; "no loss at all" therefore needs strong evidence. Test one: fix the same history (teacher forcing) and compare, at each step, the probability distributions (for example with KL divergence) or the perplexity under 8-bit and 4-bit KV, covering short, medium and long contexts. Test two: compare output quality on the same set of real tasks (long-document Q&A, code edits, multi-turn chat, "needle in a haystack"), with the tolerance and the failure cases written down in advance. The upstream docs report that 4-bit KV halves the memory and runs about 4% faster at 128K, but perplexity on long documents rises by 8%–12%, while the needle-in-a-haystack test still passes. So it is a trade-off with a cost, not lossless.

title: Performance first principles: bandwidth, compute, and critical path
deck: Why does a high-powered GPU produce tokens so slowly? Three ways to measure where the time goes.
prereq: Chapters 3 and 4. Understanding "bytes per second" is enough.
goals: Use "latency + data size ÷ bandwidth" and roofline to lower-bound a computation's time
Explain why decode is bandwidth-limited but prefill uses the full compute throughput
Apply Amdahl's law and critical path to decide if an optimization is worth doing

quiz.text: One step takes 20% of one token's time. You speed it up 2×. How much faster is the whole system?
choices: about 1.11×
quiz.why: Amdahl's law: new time = 0.8 + 0.2 ÷ 2 = 0.9, so overall speedup = 1 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 1.11×. Even infinite speedup caps at 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25×.

quiz.text: Decoding one token at a time, weights in FP16. What is the bottleneck?
choices: Not enough compute
Not enough bandwidth to move data
Disk too slow
quiz.why: Each weight does 2 operations but moves 2 bytes, so intensity ≈ 1, far left of the ridge. Most of the GPU is idle waiting for data.

quiz.text: In Strata, while the CPU computes unmatched experts on one layer, can the GPU start the next layer?
choices: Yes, GPU starts when idle
No, the next layer needs this layer's merged output
Depends on VRAM size
quiz.why: Layers are strictly serial through the residual chain. The source comment says the CPU phase "cannot be hidden" in that chain; the fix is to put more experts in VRAM cache.

problem: Teaching scenario: generating one token requires reading 0.6 GB from main memory; sustained memory bandwidth is 40 GB/s. What is the lower bound on transfer time? Can you conclude "this machine generates 66.7 tokens per second"? Why or why not?
answer: Lower bound is 0.6 ÷ 40 = 0.015 seconds, or 15 ms; reciprocal is 66.7. But this is only the lower bound for "this one read": it does not account for GPU arithmetic, other data transfers, kernel launch overhead, CPU–GPU synchronization, sampling, or the non-overlappable dependency chain. Real speed might be lower; it could also be higher if some data sits in faster VRAM or speculative decoding produces more than one token per step. So this can only be called "theoretical lower bound for this transfer", never "end-to-end speed" and certainly not "measured".

title: Model loading: from a file to tensors you can trust
deck: Opening a file, reading it into memory and proving the bytes are right are three different things.
prereq: The memory hierarchy from Chapter 1; arrays and shapes from Chapter 3; quantization formats from Chapter 4 (knowing "how many bits each number takes" is enough).
goals: Explain how mmap, page faults and the page cache relate, and why "the mapping succeeded" does not mean "the data is in RAM"
Write the overflow-safe range check o ≤ F and n ≤ F − o, and show how the addition form can be fooled
Tell checksums from cryptographic hashes, and name the steps where Strata checks its bytes

quiz.text: You map a 30 GB model file with mmap. Right after the call returns, which statement is most accurate?
choices: All 30 GB have been read into RAM
Only the mapping between addresses and the file exists; data is read in on first access
The file has been copied into VRAM
quiz.why: mmap only records the mapping. The first access to a page causes a page fault; only then does the operating system read that page from the SSD and keep it in the page cache.

quiz.text: With 8-bit unsigned integers, the file length is F = 128 and a tensor has offset o = 200 and length n = 100. Which check wrongly lets it through?
choices: o + n ≤ F
o ≤ F and n ≤ F − o
Both let it through
quiz.why: 200 + 100 = 300 goes past 255 and wraps to 44; 44 ≤ 128 holds, so the out-of-bounds tensor gets through. The safe form checks o ≤ F first, which already fails, so it rejects at once.

quiz.text: Two neighboring bytes in a downloaded file have swapped places. Which check is most likely to miss it?
choices: A checksum that adds up all the bytes
A SHA-256 hash
A byte-by-byte comparison with the original
quiz.why: Addition does not care about order, so swapping two bytes leaves the sum unchanged. SHA-256 is extremely sensitive to any change, and a byte-by-byte comparison catches it too, of course.

problem: An early version of Strata gave a "random access" hint when it opened the expert file on Windows. Speed dropped to 1.93 GB/s, each token took 344 ms, and it never warmed up. Explain why using how the page cache works, and say why "expert choices look random" does not mean "suited to a random access hint".
answer: The "random access" hint makes the system turn off read-ahead and drop pages it has read as soon as it can, because it assumes that in a big file read at random, what was read will not be read again. But the expert file is accessed like this: the experts each token picks are scattered, yet the bytes read for one token are almost all read again for the next. A cache's value depends on whether what was read gets read again (reuse), not on whether a single access is sequential. With pages dropped as fast as they come in, every access becomes a page fault and speed falls to SSD level. The right approach is to give no hint and let the page cache keep the pages that are used again and again; with enough RAM, go further and copy the experts into RAM and lock the pages.

title: One model layer: normalization, residuals and module contracts
deck: 48 editors take turns writing suggested changes in the margin: how one layer reads, computes and writes back.
prereq: Matrix multiplication from Chapter 3; the idea of experts from Chapter 10 (you can also come back to it when you reach MoE).
goals: Explain the two halves of a layer: read the residual → mixer or MoE → write back, and tell which layers are QSA and which are GDN
Compute L2 and RMS normalization by hand, and explain why the two differ by a factor of √d
Give an example of an interface error that is "right in shape, normal in value, wrong in meaning", and explain how a combination test catches it

quiz.text: Strata's rule is "layers with number % 4 == 3 are QSA layers", with layers numbered from 0. Which statement is right?
choices: A QSA layer comes once every 3 layers
The last layer of every group of 4 is QSA, 12 of the 48 layers in all
Only layer 3 is QSA
quiz.why: The layer numbers with remainder 3 are 3, 7, 11 … 47, and zero-based 3 is the 4th layer when people count. So it is once every 4 layers, 12 layers in all; the other 36 are GDN.

quiz.text: x = [3, 4]. L2 normalization gives [0.6, 0.8]. About what does RMS normalization give?
choices: [0.6, 0.8], the same as L2
About [0.85, 1.13], √2 times the L2 result
About [0.3, 0.4], half the L2 result
quiz.why: RMS = √((9 + 16) ÷ 2) ≈ 3.54, so 3 ÷ 3.54 ≈ 0.85 and 4 ÷ 3.54 ≈ 1.13. L2 divides by 5 and RMS divides by 5 ÷ √2, so RMS is √2 times larger; in d dimensions it is √d times larger.

quiz.text: An expert's routing weight is 0.2. If the expert pool has already multiplied by 0.2 once and the combine step multiplies again, what is this expert's final coefficient?
quiz.why: 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04, so the contribution is wrongly shrunk 5×. The result is still a normal number and raises no error, so the defenses are the contract (multiply only once, at the combine) and whole-layer comparison tests.

problem: Why can a set of unit tests in which "every operator is correct on its own" still not prove that a layer is right? Give an example using one of the contracts in this chapter, and say what tests should be added.
answer: Unit tests check only each operator's output for given inputs; they cannot check "who is responsible for what" between operators. For example, GDN's single-step kernel expects the β it receives to have already passed through sigmoid; if the layer forgets to do it, the kernel still computes a row of normal numbers and every unit test passes. In the same way, routing weights applied once by the expert pool and again by the combine step, the previous layer's expert results paired with this layer's weights, or L2 and RMS normalization mixed up all produce only "plausible-looking" numbers. Add combination tests: fix the input and the history state, and compare the whole-layer output, plus intermediate checkpoints such as the half-layer outputs and inject, item by item against an independent reference implementation. Strata's per-layer residual record and half-layer record exist for exactly this purpose.

title: Attention, GQA and sparse selection
deck: Looking back through the book with a question: how attention is computed, why it gets pricier as text grows, and how Strata's model looks at a little less.
prereq: Softmax from Chapter 2; vector dot products from Chapter 3; "the skeleton of a layer" from Chapter 7.
goals: Compute one attention step by hand: dot-product scores, divide by √d, softmax, weighted sum
Explain the causal mask and O(n²), and use 12 layers × 2 KV heads × 256 dimensions to show that the KV cache for a 32K context is 768 MiB
Explain why QSA's "at most 2051 positions per step" and "all the KV must still be kept" are both true, and tell optimizations that only change the location from those that change the set

quiz.text: Two earlier positions have values [2, 0] and [0, 4], and both scaled scores are 0. What is the attention output?
quiz.why: The two scores are equal, so softmax gives weights ½ and ½, and the output = ½ × [2, 0] + ½ × [0, 4] = [1, 2]. Attention mixes in proportion; it neither picks one nor simply adds them up.

quiz.text: Each QSA layer in Strata's model has 24 query heads and 2 KV heads. Which head count do you multiply by when sizing the KV cache?
quiz.why: The cache stores keys and values, and the 24 query heads share these 2 sets. So each token stores 2 × 256 × 2 (K and V) × 2 bytes = 2 KiB per layer, 24,576 bytes across the 12 layers.

quiz.text: QSA looks at no more than 2051 positions for each token it generates. Can we therefore keep only the KV of the last 2051 tokens?
choices: Yes, it never looks at more than that
No, the next token may pick any old position
Yes, as long as the context is under 262K
quiz.why: Each step looks at a picked working set, not a fixed window of the most recent tokens. Different queries pick different old positions, so all the KV must be kept; it can be moved to RAM, but not deleted.

problem: How many MiB are 805,306,368 bytes? The comment in Strata's qsa.hpp writes it as "805 MiB". What is wrong with that? In a VRAM and RAM budget of tens of GB, how large an error can this kind of mix-up cause?
answer: 805,306,368 ÷ 2^20 = 768 MiB. 805 is the decimal MB you get by dividing by 10^6; the comment treats MB as MiB. 1 MiB = 1.048576 MB, so the two differ by about 4.9%; GiB and GB differ by about 7.4%. In a budget of 12 GB of VRAM and tens of GB of RAM, that means an error of hundreds of MB to several GB, enough to decide "can we fit a few hundred more experts" or "will we run out of VRAM". When you budget capacity, write the unit for every item, and stick to either powers of 2 or powers of 10.

title: GDN: remembering the history in a fixed-size state
deck: No flipping through notes, just erasing and rewriting a whiteboard: how the outer product, the Delta rule and gated decay squeeze the history into a 128 × 128 matrix.
prereq: Dot products and matrices from Chapter 3; L2 normalization and sigmoid from Chapter 7; attention from Chapter 8 (for comparison).
goals: Write a rank-one update with an outer product, and explain why the same key reads the value back
Work one step of a one-dimensional GDN by hand, and explain why "decay, then write" and the reverse give different results
Show that the state of the 36 GDN layers is about 112 MiB and does not grow with the context, and explain why it cannot simply be rolled back

quiz.text: The whiteboard is all 0. With key [1, 0], first write [2, 3], then write [5, 1]. What do the Delta rule (α = β = 1) and plain addition each read back?
choices: Both read back [5, 1]
The Delta rule reads back [5, 1], plain addition reads back [7, 4]
The Delta rule reads back [7, 4], plain addition reads back [5, 1]
quiz.why: Before the second write, the Delta rule reads out the old value [2, 3] and writes only the difference [3, −2], so the first row becomes [5, 1]. Plain addition adds [5, 1] straight onto [2, 3], giving [7, 4].

quiz.text: How big is the main state of the 36 GDN layers in Strata's model (128 × 128 × 48 FP32 numbers per layer) in total?
choices: 108 MiB, regardless of context length
108 GiB
108 MiB per token
quiz.why: Each layer is 128 × 128 × 48 × 4 bytes = 3 MiB, so 36 layers make 108 MiB; add about 4.2 MiB of convolution history. It is this size from the very first token and does not grow with the context.

quiz.text: Within one token, different columns of the whiteboard can be computed in parallel. Does this mean different tokens can also update the state at the same time, independently?
choices: Yes, all tokens can be computed together
No, step t + 1 needs the state from step t
It depends on whether there are enough threads
quiz.why: The parallelism is over the columns within one step: each column reads and writes only itself. Along time it is a chain: the new state depends on the old one, so it must go step by step.

problem: Using this chapter's one-dimensional example (S = 2, α = 0.5, k = 1, v = 3, β = 0.25), explain why, after speculative decoding rejects a draft word, you cannot just move the position counter back. How does Strata handle it?
answer: Once the draft word has gone through GDN, it has already rewritten the state from 2 to 1.5; moving the position counter back does not turn the state back into 2. Nor can the recurrence generally be run backward: both the decay and the Delta write erase part of the old information. The right approach is to save a snapshot, or to start from a state known to be correct and replay only the accepted words. Strata's verify window leaves the GDN state untouched during the check; once it is settled that the first n words are accepted, it replays those n words from the inputs saved in the window, pushing the recurrent state and the convolution history forward. The KV cache is different: the keys and values at rejected positions are simply overwritten when those positions are processed later.

title: MoE: why huge models run on small graphics cards
deck: Having many parameters does not mean using many parameters at every step.
prereq: Chapter 1. Knowing what a token and VRAM are is enough; Chapters 3 and 4 help with the "Go deeper" section.
goals: Explain what an expert is and how the router picks experts
Estimate how many parameters one token really uses
Explain how Strata splits the experts between the GPU and RAM

quiz.text: Each layer has 512 experts and picks only 10 each time. Can we just delete the experts that were not picked?
choices: Yes, they were not used this time anyway
No, the next token may need them
Only if the router is accurate enough
quiz.why: Sparse computation is not permanent pruning. Deleting experts changes the model itself; the upstream Coder version dropped half of the experts and got clearly weaker at Chinese.

quiz.text: If more experts are cached on the GPU, what usually happens to generation speed?
choices: It goes up: the CPU has fewer missed experts to compute
No change: speed depends only on GPU compute
It goes down: VRAM is fuller
quiz.why: In upstream measurements, raising the experts on the GPU from 1,589 to 3,872 lifted the speed from 50.9 to 62.6 tokens per second.

quiz.text: The 10th and 11th experts differ in score by only 0.0001. What can a tiny numerical error in the computation do?
choices: Nothing, the error is too small
It can swap out a whole expert
The output will also differ by only 0.0001
quiz.why: Top-k is a discontinuous boundary: however small the score gap, once the ranking flips, a different expert takes part in the computation.

problem: You have a 12 GB graphics card and plan to switch to a 24 GB one. Using "each extra 1 GB of VRAM holds about 700 more experts", how many more experts can you cache? Will speed necessarily rise in proportion? List at least two factors that could make the estimate wrong.
answer: The extra 12 GB holds about 12 × 700 = 8,400 more experts. But speed will not rise in proportion: (1) VRAM must also hold the chat history (KV), the weights used at every step such as attention, and scratch buffers, and a long context eats more VRAM; (2) the gain depends on the hit rate: when the hot experts are already on the GPU, the new ones are mostly cold, so returns diminish; (3) the bottleneck may move to the CPU, RAM bandwidth or the GPU's own compute; (4) experts differ in size across quantization formats, so the count per GB differs too. The only way to know the real gain is to measure with a fixed model, context length and workload.

title: PLE and n-grams: the model looks things up in a big table too
deck: Hashing to row numbers, reading the SSD by page, an 8-way set-associative row cache: how a 28.8 GB table gives up only 16 rows per token.
prereq: Chapter 1 (memory hierarchy) and Chapter 10 (intuition for experts and caching). A little binary helps.
goals: Explain what an n-gram is, and how three tokens become 16 row numbers through hashing (multiply, XOR, take the remainder)
Work out the cost of reading by page: why a 90-byte row needs a 4 KiB read, and why a row that crosses a page boundary needs two pages
Use set-associative caches and a rotating pointer to explain conflict misses: why a cache with enough total capacity can still keep missing

quiz.text: When a set in Strata's PLE row cache is full, which row gets replaced?
choices: The row that has gone unused the longest
The row under this set's replacement pointer; then the pointer moves on by one
A row picked at random
quiz.why: The source gives each set a rotating pointer: the new row is written into the way the pointer points at, the pointer adds one, and after a full round it wraps to the start. It does not track which row was used most recently, so it is not LRU.

quiz.text: A row is 200 bytes and starts at byte 4000 of a page (4096 bytes). Reading whole pages, how many pages must be read?
choices: 1 page
2 pages
200 pages
quiz.why: 4000 + 200 = 4200, past the page's end at 4096. The row reaches into the next page, so both pages must be read.

quiz.text: Two different trigrams hash to the same row. What happens?
choices: The program reports an error and refuses to run
Both read the same row data; this is a collision accepted by design
The program automatically stores one of them in an empty row instead
quiz.why: The table stores only values, not keys, so it neither notices nor handles collisions. There are far more combinations than rows, so collisions are certain. Different heads use different moduli, so two n-grams rarely collide on every head.

problem: A program hands its SSD reads to a dedicated I/O thread. The time the main thread spends submitting requests drops to almost zero, yet the total time per token does not get shorter. Give two reasonable explanations, and say what to measure to tell them apart.
answer: Explanation 1: right after submitting, the main thread needs the data, with no other work to do in between. The waiting has only moved from "submit" to "collect"; it has not been hidden. Explanation 2: the reads themselves got slower or are held up by something else, such as the cost of waking threads and taking locks, the latency of random reads, or the same file still being memory-mapped, which serializes the reads. To tell them apart, record three timestamps for every request: submitted, completed and consumed. If completion comes well before consumption, the reads are already hidden and the bottleneck is elsewhere. If the consumer is always waiting for completion, look at the percentiles of the wait time and of the single-read latency.

title: The expert cache: whom to keep, how to split, when to swap
deck: The denominator of a hit rate, a starting list ranked by frequency, a range of slots per layer, replacement by decayed count, and the "copy first, register after" order of a swap.
prereq: Chapter 10 (the intuition behind MoE and the expert cache) and Chapter 11 (set-associative caches).
goals: Name the denominator of a hit rate, and explain why the per-expert hit rate and the whole-layer hit rate differ by more than ten times
Compare LRU, LFU and decayed counts, and state the adjustment rules of Strata's expert cache (every 4 rounds, a count of 2, a lead of 1.5, × 0.7)
Write down the correct order for one swap: remove the table entry, wait for the copy to finish, then register

quiz.text: In some layer, each expert's hit rate is 70%. If the experts were independent, about how likely is it that all 10 experts in this layer hit?
choices: About 2.8%
quiz.why: All 10 must hit: 0.7 to the 10th power ≈ 0.028. The two metrics have different denominators and cannot stand in for each other. Real routing is not independent, so the real figure has to be measured separately.

quiz.text: During an expert swap, the residency table already says "#112 is in slot 5", but the bytes are still being copied. If the GPU follows the table and computes #112 now, what happens?
choices: Nothing wrong, just a bit slower
It may read half-new, half-old bytes and compute a wrong result without any error
The program is sure to crash
quiz.why: The table entry and the bytes must be valid together. When an async copy function returns, the bytes have not necessarily arrived; registering early creates a fake hit with "right label, wrong bytes". The output looks normal, but it is already wrong.

quiz.text: The early expert cache had all layers share one counter and handed out slots in order of arrival. Its hit rate was only about 3%. What was the main reason?
choices: VRAM was too small
The early layers arrived first and took every slot, so the later layers never got any
The GPU cannot compute the later layers
quiz.why: A token walks from layer 0 onward, and 256 slots are all handed out by about layer 26. Capacity was enough; the problem was that allocation got tangled up with the access order. Giving each layer its own range of slots fixed it.

problem: In the low-RAM resident mode, RAM holds only the experts the graphics card does not have. List three conditions that one expert swap in this mode must keep.
answer: First, before the incoming expert becomes visible to the GPU (registered in the residency table), its bytes have been fully copied into the VRAM slot. Second, before its slot is overwritten, the outgoing expert has been removed from the table (the CPU computes it from then on), and its full bytes have been copied back to RAM, into the place the incoming expert used to hold, so the RAM copy keeps exactly filling in what the GPU is missing. Third, table changes are synchronized with concurrent readers: any token that picks either expert during the copy must take the CPU path and must never see a half-new, half-old state. You should also check that expert blocks never cross slot boundaries, that errors can roll back, and that the RAM budget is not exceeded.

title: CPU + GPU: parallel within a layer, in line across layers
deck: Computing an expert is mostly reading bytes. Hits go to the GPU and misses to the CPU, both at once; data dependence sets the critical path.
prereq: Chapter 5 (intuition for bandwidth and the critical path), Chapter 10 (MoE) and Chapter 12 (the expert cache).
goals: Describe how CPUs and GPUs are designed differently, and use the SIMD example to explain why only independent data can be computed at once
Explain why Strata lets the CPU compute missed experts in place, and draw the timeline of how the GPU and CPU share one layer
Use data dependence and the critical path to explain why layers cannot run in parallel, and why cutting work that is not on the critical path does nothing

quiz.text: The two branches are independent. The CPU branch has an effective rate Bc = 40 and the PCIe branch Bp = 20. To make both finish at the same time, what fraction f should go to the PCIe branch?
quiz.why: Set the two times equal: (1 − f)/40 = f/20, which gives f = 20 ÷ (40 + 20) = 1/3. The slower branch should get the smaller share.

quiz.text: While the CPU is still computing layer l's experts, can the GPU start computing layer l + 1?
choices: Always
No, layer l + 1's input must wait for layer l to finish merging
Yes, as long as there are enough threads
quiz.why: Layer l + 1's input is exactly layer l's result after its 10 experts are merged. That is a data dependence. No scheduler, however clever, can get around it; the 48 layers form one serial chain.

quiz.text: Upstream cut the CPU's expert work per token from 18.2 milliseconds to 10.2 milliseconds, yet the total time per token did not change. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The CPU measurement was wrong
The GPU's share of the work was queued behind the CPU, so the critical path stayed just as long
Not enough VRAM
quiz.why: In the first version, the GPU step that computes the hit experts ran after the CPU expert pool, so the GPU's share filled the time the CPU saved. Only after both sides computed at once did it really get faster.

problem: Build an example where giving a larger share to the GPU makes the whole thing slower. Explain it with the times of the two branches.
answer: Say that in some layer the CPU branch takes 8 milliseconds and the GPU branch over PCIe takes 7 milliseconds, so the join is set by the CPU's 8 milliseconds. Move more missed experts to the GPU: the CPU drops to 4 milliseconds, but the GPU branch grows to 12 milliseconds (PCIe transfer is slow), so the join now comes at 12 milliseconds, slower than before. If you also account for the CPU reading experts and PCIe reading pinned memory sharing the same memory bandwidth, a longer GPU branch also slows the CPU down, and things get even worse. The best point is where the two branches finish at the same time, not "the more GPU, the better".

title: Pinned memory, DMA and async: copy while you compute
deck: Virtual addresses can move, but DMA trusts only physical addresses; "submitted" does not mean "done"; double buffering is correct only thanks to two signals.
prereq: Chapter 6 (files and memory mapping), Chapter 12 (swapping experts in the cache), Chapter 13 (how the CPU and GPU split the work).
goals: Use virtual memory and paging to explain why DMA needs pinned memory and why Strata pins tens of GB at startup
Tell synchronous from asynchronous calls, and name two "returned does not mean done" examples in Strata (cache fills, verify window commits)
Compute the total time of double buffering and state what makes it correct: read only after the copy is done, write only after it has been used

quiz.text: An asynchronous copy function has returned. What does that tell you?
choices: The data has definitely reached its destination
The copy has been submitted, not necessarily finished
The source buffer can be freed right away
quiz.why: An asynchronous call only hands the work off. Whether the data has arrived, and whether the source buffer can be changed, depends on the completion event, not on whether the function has returned.

quiz.text: Two buffers, 4 chunks, each chunk takes 3 milliseconds to copy and 5 to compute, and copy and compute use independent hardware. What is the ideal total time?
choices: 20 milliseconds
23 milliseconds
32 milliseconds
quiz.why: The first copy takes 3 milliseconds, the 3 steps in between each cost the slower compute, 5 milliseconds, and the last compute takes 5: 3 + 3 × 5 + 5 = 23. Only a fully serial run takes 4 × 8 = 32.

quiz.text: The GPU can read a block of pinned memory directly through a mapping. Does that mean the data is already in VRAM?
choices: Yes
No, every read still goes over PCIe
Only on Windows
quiz.why: "An address the GPU can access" and "where the data actually lives" are two different things. Mapped pinned memory still sits in the host's RAM; the GPU reads it over PCIe and is limited by the bus bandwidth.

problem: A program sometimes reads the previous round's old state when it saves a checkpoint. Someone added "wait 0.1 seconds" before the save, and the problem went away. Why is this not a reliable fix? What should be done instead?
answer: A fixed wait does not create an explicit "read only after the write is done" relationship. On a slower machine, under resource contention, or when this round has more data, 0.1 seconds may not be enough and the problem comes back; on a fast machine it just wastes time. The right fix is to wait for the completion signal tied to that state write, such as an event recorded after the write, or the wait_commit() that Strata's verifier provides, and to handle a failed or timed-out wait.

title: GPU kernels, fusion and CUDA Graph
deck: Every kernel launch pays a check-in fee: how do you check in less without freezing the position?
prereq: Chapters 1, 5 and 13 (the memory hierarchy, bandwidth, and how the CPU and GPU differ).
goals: Explain how threads, thread blocks and warps divide the work, and why neighboring threads should read neighboring addresses
Use n × L + w and L + n × w to judge whether a chain of kernels is limited by launch overhead
Tell kernel fusion apart from CUDA Graph, and explain why values that change every step must live in a fixed-address buffer when you capture a graph

quiz.text: A kernel computes for only 5 microseconds, but each submission takes 20 microseconds. If you submit 45 such kernels one by one, what is the GPU doing most of the time?
choices: Computing at full load the whole time
Waiting for the CPU to submit the next kernel
Waiting for data in VRAM to move to the SSD
quiz.why: When w < L, the total is about n × L + w = 45 × 20 + 5 = 905 microseconds, of which the GPU computes only 45 × 5 = 225 microseconds; the rest is spent waiting for submissions. This is what "launch-bound" means.

quiz.text: Are CUDA Graph and kernel fusion the same thing?
choices: Yes, a graph merges all kernels into one
No: a graph saves CPU-side submission and its nodes are still the original kernels; fusion is what merges the computation into one kernel
They are the same compiler optimization under different names
quiz.why: A graph records a chain of operations and their dependencies, then submits and replays the whole chain at once, and each node still runs on its own. Fusion rewrites the kernel so intermediate results stay on chip. Strata uses both.

quiz.text: If you capture "the current position pos" into a graph as a kernel argument and then simply replay it, what happens?
choices: The driver adds one to pos automatically
Every token writes to position 0, the value at capture time; the program reports no error, but the model acts as if it has lost its memory
The graph refuses to replay and reports an error
quiz.why: A graph copies argument values at capture time, and replay never rereads them. Strata's qsa.hpp puts pos, n_kv, n_bid and width into a fixed-address step buffer; the kernels read it from VRAM every time, and the host rewrites its content each step.

problem: Design a small test that does not need the full large model and that catches the bug "sampling parameters are not updated when the graph is replayed".
answer: Fix a set of logits and send two requests in a row: the first greedy, the second at high temperature or with a different fixed random number. Run each on both the graph path and a reference path that does not use a graph, and compare the parameters each path actually used and the tokens it picked. The second request must take a branch that differs from the first and can be predicted. If you only change the random seed while the distribution is so lopsided that it always picks the same token, this test cannot reveal the bug.

title: Prefill: turning many tokens into a batch problem
deck: On the same computer, reading the prompt is more than twenty times faster than writing the answer: the secret is batching and pipelining.
prereq: Chapters 3, 5, 10 and 14 (matrix multiplication, bandwidth and arithmetic intensity, MoE experts, DMA and asynchrony).
goals: Use matrix × vector vs matrix × matrix to explain why prefill is faster than decode
Explain grouping by expert and the trade-offs of chunk size C: reuse, temporary VRAM, cancel latency
Draw the pipeline that overlaps moving and computing, and name the states that must be handed off after a chunk

quiz.text: During prefill every token of the prompt is already known. So can the 5th token "see" the 6th?
choices: Yes, they are all known anyway
No. The causal rule does not change; batching only changes how the computation is organized
Only for English prompts
quiz.why: A known input does not mean the model may look at the future. Prefill still uses the causal mask, and the recurrent layers still walk through the chunk in order.

quiz.text: Why does the dense part for 8 tokens together take only about 3 times as long as for one token, and not 8 times?
choices: Because the GPU skips half of the tokens
Because one read of the weights is shared by all 8 tokens, so the moving cost is spread thin
Because computing together uses lower precision
quiz.why: In matrix × vector, one read of the weights serves one token; in matrix × matrix, the same weights serve the whole batch. The compute is all still done, but the move is paid once. The default table in spec/controller.hpp lists 3.0× for 8 tokens.

quiz.text: During prefill, Strata puts the chunk buffer in slots borrowed from the expert cache. While prefill runs, can the experts that used to be in those slots still count as "hits"?
choices: Yes, the address has not changed
No. Their bytes have been overwritten, so they must be moved instead and filled back in after prefill
Yes, as long as the budgets add up to less than VRAM
quiz.why: The address is still there, but the content is now the chunk buffer. The safety condition is that at every moment the label matches the bytes in the slot: while lent out they do not count as hits, and only after the refill finishes may they be announced again.

problem: The same prompt is read once with C = 1 and once with C = 8192, and the final answers are not word-for-word identical. Why can you neither conclude right away that one side has a bug, nor wave it off with "it's just floating point"?
answer: Batched and one-by-one computation can take different rounding paths (upstream has documented that IQ models round differently in the single-token and multi-token expert kernels), and a tiny logits difference can make some token branch off. But the difference can also come from a real error in the state handoff, the causal mask or the layout. Compare on the same fixed history: the intermediate tensors, the chosen experts and index numbers, and the layer where the error starts to grow. Then judge by tolerances and quality gates set in advance. Check the non-numeric contracts, such as state positions, the mask and index numbers, separately and exactly.

title: KV capacity, working sets and tiered storage
deck: How many bytes does it take to remember a conversation, is that GB or GiB, and does it live in VRAM or RAM?
prereq: Chapters 1, 4, 8 and 12 (memory hierarchy, quantization, attention, cache replacement).
goals: Compute the KV bytes of one conversation as 12 layers × 2 heads × 256 dimensions × 2 × bytes per element
Tell GB (10⁹) from GiB (2³⁰), and spot errors where the number and the unit do not match
Explain the page table and KV streaming: VRAM holds only the pages in use, the full history is in RAM, and misses are swapped in with CLOCK

quiz.text: When Strata stores KV in FP16, how big is the main KV for a 128K (131,072-token) context?
choices: Exactly 3 GiB
12 GiB
108 MiB
quiz.why: 12 layers × 2 heads × 256 dimensions × 2 (K, V) × 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes per token; times 131,072 that is 3,221,225,472 bytes, exactly 3 × 2³⁰, which is 3 GiB (about 3.22 GB).

quiz.text: How should you write 805,306,368 bytes?
choices: 805 MiB
805 MB, which is 768 MiB
768 MB
quiz.why: Divide by 10⁶ to get 805.3 MB, or by 2²⁰ to get 768 MiB. A comment in Strata's source writes "805 MiB", pairing the decimal number with the binary unit.

quiz.text: A 256K conversation runs with KV streaming on, and VRAM keeps the KV of only 32,768 positions. Can the model still see the earlier content?
choices: No, the earlier history has been deleted
Yes: the full history is in RAM, and selected pages are swapped into VRAM before they are read
It can see only 1 in every 4 tokens
quiz.why: Being resident and being kept are two different things. The upstream docs say that with streaming, attention reads exactly the same values; only where the KV lives changes. How much stays in VRAM affects only speed.

problem: A report counts Strata's KV over 48 layers and says "this is a conservative estimate, so it is fine". Why does the report still fail?
answer: Only the 12 QSA layers have KV, so counting 48 layers makes the result 4 times too big. Erring on the safe side is not the same as having the right model: a false attribution makes people misjudge the bottleneck, buy the wrong hardware or switch off useful features. Count with the real 12 layers, then list the margin as its own item, instead of passing off a structural error as margin.

title: Speculative decoding: guess boldly, commit strictly
deck: Guess a few tokens, then verify them in one go: how is a wrong guess taken back, and why does the answer stay the same?
prereq: Chapters 2, 9, 14 and 16 (sampling and random numbers, the GDN recurrent state, synchronous versus asynchronous, batching).
goals: State the rule "accept up to the first mismatch" and explain why every draft after it is thrown away
Map speculative decoding onto CPU branch prediction and speculative execution
Say, state by state, how GDN, the indexer, PLE and KV are taken back when the first a + 1 rows are committed

quiz.text: In the window, the 2nd draft differs from the target's pick, and the 3rd draft happens to match the original text. Can the 3rd one be accepted?
choices: Yes, it is right
No, it was guessed after a wrong word, so its premise no longer holds
It depends on how long the window is
quiz.why: Correctness holds as a chain along the prefix: a later draft has a correct premise only if everything before it matched. Strata's loop while (window[a+1] == outv[a]) ++a stops at the first mismatch.

quiz.text: With temperature sampling on, how does Strata decide by default whether a draft can be accepted?
choices: The draft writes for the target directly, with no verification
Only if it exactly equals the target's reproducible sampled result for this row
Accept it with probability min(1, p/q)
quiz.why: Each row's random number is set by the seed and the absolute position, and the draft must equal the target's sampled result for that row. This is Strata's default rule. min(1, p/q) is the classic paper's method; since v0.1.40.2 Strata can use it too, but only if you set STRATA_SPEC_PROB=1 by hand.

quiz.text: A window accepted only 1 draft. Is it enough to just roll back the position counter?
choices: Yes
No: GDN must replay, the indexer must restore a snapshot, and PLE must restore the matching snapshot
Only KV needs handling
quiz.why: Different states are taken back in different ways. The extra KV slots actually need nothing and wait to be overwritten next round; GDN, the indexer and PLE each return to the prefix state in their own way.

problem: You want to add a "per-sequence statistics buffer" to Strata (for example, one that counts how often each token has appeared). Write a speculative-decoding safety checklist for it.
answer: ① Which range of the history it covers; ② whether the verify window writes it tentatively while running; ③ whether it needs a snapshot, replay of recorded inputs, or is naturally overwritable; ④ how commit(n_keep) makes it reflect only the first n_keep rows (note n_keep = accepted drafts + 1); ⑤ how the rejected part is invalidated; ⑥ who confirms that asynchronous reads and writes have finished, and with which event (for example wait_commit after an asynchronous commit); ⑦ how it is cleaned up on an end token, a cancellation or a session restore; ⑧ compare it item by item with the reference result without speculation under the same fixed history.

title: How many drafts to guess: expected value, cost and learning on the fly
deck: A correctly guessed token is free, but verification takes time. How many guesses pay off best, and what if the acceptance rate changes?
prereq: Chapter 18 (speculative decoding and commit). Chapter 10's expert cache helps but is not required.
goals: Use conditional acceptance rates to compute the expected tokens committed per round, and explain why extra guesses give diminishing returns
Explain why you compare "expected tokens committed per millisecond" rather than the acceptance rate or the window length
Estimate a changing acceptance rate with an exponential moving average, and handle draft positions that were never compared correctly

quiz.text: Three drafts have conditional acceptance rates 0.8, 0.6 and 0.5. How many tokens does one round commit on average?
quiz.why: E = 1 + 0.8 + 0.8×0.6 + 0.8×0.6×0.5 = 1 + 0.8 + 0.48 + 0.24 = 2.52. The leading 1 is the big model's own token; draft i is useful only if the first i are all accepted.

quiz.text: A round guessed 3 and the 1st was rejected right away. How should the estimate for position 3 be updated?
choices: Record a failure
Do not update: it was never compared this round
Record a success
quiz.why: Once the 1st draft is rejected, later positions are not compared; the outcome is "not seen". Recording a failure drags the deep positions' estimates down, and the controller wrongly concludes long windows do not pay. Strata's observe updates only the accepted positions and the first rejected one.

quiz.text: When the controller picks a window length, which number does it really want to maximize?
choices: The number of drafts
The drafts' acceptance rate
Expected tokens committed ÷ time per round
quiz.why: The goal is more tokens per millisecond. As the window grows, the expected token count grows more and more slowly while the round time keeps rising, so speed has a peak. A high acceptance rate with more expensive rounds can still be slower overall.

problem: Strata's controller updates acceptance rates with an exponential moving average using α = 0.05. What would happen with α = 0.5 instead? Explain in terms of reaction speed and noise, and compute the half-life for both values of α.
answer: Half-life = ln 0.5 ÷ ln(1 − α). That is about 13.5 rounds for α = 0.05 and exactly 1 round for α = 0.5. With α = 0.5 the estimate catches up almost immediately after a topic change, but every acceptance or rejection makes it jump a lot (the steady-state standard deviation is about √(α ÷ (2 − α) × p(1 − p)), which at p = 0.86 rises from about 0.056 to about 0.20). The controller would change windows constantly, and a few chance rejections could even push the estimate below the threshold and stop drafting. Looking only at Controller's two functions, once drafting stops there are no new observations, so the estimate can never recover. α is a trade-off between "react fast" and "do not get fooled by noise".

title: Prefix reuse, snapshots and copy-on-write
deck: Why does a follow-up answer almost instantly? The engine saved the prefix it already read. But "the same question" is not "the same state", and saving the KV is not saving the whole conversation.
prereq: Chapters 9, 17 and 18. Knowing what the KV cache and recurrent state are is enough.
goals: Name the four conditions prefix reuse must meet: steering mode, length, tokens and image identity
Explain why the KV cache can roll back by "ignoring the later rows" while the recurrent state can only roll back through checkpoints
Use copy-on-write to count how many pages two branches sharing a prefix must copy, and state what Strata actually does

quiz.text: Two requests have exactly the same token IDs; only the image attached to the second one is different. Will Strata reuse the first one's checkpoint?
choices: Yes, the tokens are the same
No, the image's position and hash must also match
Yes, as long as both images have the same size
quiz.why: In the token sequence an image is just a run of placeholders, and identical placeholders can stand for completely different pictures. The engine records each image's start position and content hash separately; a different hash means no reuse.

quiz.text: You want to take a conversation back to its state at token 4. Which kind of memory can roll back by simply "ignoring what comes after", and which cannot?
choices: The KV cache can, the GDN recurrent state cannot
Both can
The GDN recurrent state can, the KV cache cannot
quiz.why: The KV cache appends one row per position, and the later rows will be overwritten later, so ignoring them works. The GDN recurrent state is rewritten whole and in place for every token, so its old form is gone; only a checkpoint saved in advance can bring it back.

quiz.text: The prefix has 17 tokens at 4 per page, and after the fork both A and B keep writing. With copy-on-write, how many KV pages must at least be copied after the fork?
choices: 0 pages
1 page
5 pages
quiz.why: The first 4 pages are full and only read, never written, so they can be shared. Page 5 holds only 1 prefix token and both sides will write into it, so whoever writes first must copy it. Only a full copy would need 5 pages.

problem: Design a minimal experiment that needs no GPU to check whether "session A saves a snapshot, switches to run B, then restores A" leaks state between the sessions.
answer: Use a deterministic toy recurrence (for example s ← 0.5s + t). Give A and B the same prefix, then different suffixes, and advance them in turns: run A a few steps and save a snapshot, switch to B, then restore A and continue. At every step compare A's and B's states bit for bit with the result of "replaying each one independently from the start"; they must be exactly equal. Then add some failures: A is cancelled midway and B continues, a snapshot is truncated, a snapshot has the wrong format, the budget is too small. The correct response is to refuse clearly and keep the original state, not to carry on computing with half a state.

title: Two graphics cards: layer split, pipelining and handoff
deck: Two graphics cards first solve "it does not fit", not "it is too slow": a token still queues layer by layer, and the pipeline only starts turning while reading the prompt.
prereq: Chapters 1, 5, 10 and 16; having read Chapter 18's "verify window" helps.
goals: Tell apart what a layer split, tensor parallelism and request parallelism each save and each cost
Use a + b + (N − 1) × max(a, b) to compute a pipeline's total time and its bubbles
Estimate the cost of a handoff from the bytes, the number of crossings and the bandwidth

quiz.text: The first card needs 4 ms for its layers and the second 5 ms, ignoring transfers. Generating just one token, what is the fastest it can take?
choices: 5 ms
9 ms
4.5 ms
quiz.why: The same token must finish the first card's layers before it can enter the second card, so the two parts can only run one after the other: 4 + 5 = 9 ms. The two cards cannot work on the same token at once.

quiz.text: Still 4 ms and 5 ms, the prompt is cut into 8 chunks, and the two cards read staggered. About how long does it take?
choices: 44 ms
72 ms
40 ms
quiz.why: The slower card sets the beat: total = 4 + 5 + (8 − 1) × 5 = 44 ms. 72 ms is chunk after chunk in sequence; 40 ms ignores the fill bubble at the start.

quiz.text: Why does Strata's two-card mode not need NVLink?
choices: It crosses cards only once per verify window, with only a few hundred KB of data
It splits every layer's matrices across both cards and computes them at the same time
Each card serves different users and they never talk
quiz.why: Strata uses a layer split: a token crosses cards once per verify window, 51,216 bytes per token, relayed through RAM, and PCIe is enough. Syncing at every layer is what tensor parallelism does, and that is what needs a fast interconnect.

problem: A friend says: "I added a second graphics card and prompt reading got 20% faster, which shows the layer-split pipeline is very efficient." What is loose about this reasoning? How would you measure it?
answer: The extra VRAM can cache more experts and cut CPU work, which by itself speeds things up and has nothing to do with the pipeline. Measure separately: each card's expert hit rate, the CPU pool's workload, the handoff time, and each stage's time per chunk. Then use a + b + (N − 1) × max(a, b) to estimate the pure pipeline's theoretical gain and compare it with the measurement. You can also compare with "no split when one card is enough" (upstream's split_skip_if_fits switch) to see how much comes from capacity and how much from the pipeline.

title: Portability: one source tree, different machines
deck: A chip understands only its own instructions. One source tree must be compiled once for each kind of machine, and "it compiles" is still several levels of evidence away from "it is supported".
prereq: Chapters 10 and 13. Knowing that the GPU and the CPU split the expert computation is enough; Chapter 4's floating-point rounding helps with Section 22.4.
goals: Explain what the compiler, the instruction set and conditional compilation each do, and read a block of #if branches
Explain how Strata picks AVX-512 / AVX2 kernels at run time on the CPU, and how it builds CUDA-style source into a HIP engine
Tell apart four levels of evidence (compiles, tests pass, runs on a real card, maintainer verified) and write a support statement that does not overclaim

quiz.text: Strata adds the AVX-512 compile switch only to a few kernel source files, not to the whole program. What is the main reason?
choices: To make compiling faster
So the CPU probe and the fallback code can run safely on CPUs without AVX-512
Because AVX-512 instructions may appear in only one file
quiz.why: Once a file is compiled with the AVX-512 switch, the compiler may insert AVX-512 instructions anywhere in it. Keeping the probe and the fallback in files without the switch lets an old CPU safely "ask first" and then decide which path to take.

quiz.text: How does Strata's HIP build get CUDA-style source to compile for AMD cards?
choices: A tool permanently rewrites every source file into HIP
At compile time it force-includes a shim header whose macros rename cuda-prefixed names to hip names, and it hand-writes a few built-in functions HIP lacks
AMD cards can run NVIDIA machine code directly
quiz.why: The build script uses -include to push hip_compat/cuda_runtime.h into every source file; it holds 91 lines of #define renaming, and built-ins such as __dp4a and warp shuffles are implemented separately per GPU architecture in intrinsics.hpp. The source itself is not changed.

quiz.text: gfx1102 compiles and passes Strata's built-in tests, and one user ran a complete model on an RX 7600 XT, but the build script still lists it as unverified. By this chapter's evidence levels, which statement is most accurate?
choices: It is fully supported
It has compiling, tests, and one user's report of a complete run, but there is only one report and the maintainer did not reproduce it, so it still counts as unverified
It cannot be used because it is on no list
quiz.why: The build script lists gfx1102 as unverified: it compiles, and configuring prints a warning. Passing tests shows the kernels do not crash and compute correctly. One user running a complete model is stronger evidence, but it is only one report. It counts as maintainer-verified only when someone can reproduce it and someone owns it.

problem: You added a new GPU backend to Strata and ran one decode successfully on one card with one model pack. Write a support statement that does not overclaim, listing at least the build conditions to record, the scope that was verified, and the parts explicitly not tested.
answer: Build conditions: the source commit, the compiler and its version, the list of target architectures, every compile switch, the dependency library versions (such as the pinned ggml commit), and the runtime environment variables. Verified scope: the device model and driver, the model pack and quantization format, the KV format, whether only decode or also prefill was tested, the context length and how many tokens were run; label the evidence level clearly as "compiles", "built-in tests pass", "tensor-level error against a reference implementation" or "end-to-end quality". Untested parts: list other architectures, other model packs, long contexts, multiple GPUs, another operating system and so on, one by one, as "untested". Do not write "fully supported", and do not promise bit-identical results with other backends.

title: From tokens to an API: templates, SSE and tool calls
deck: An answer that appears word by word depends on three gates that each "collect first, then process".
prereq: Chapter 1 (tokens and tokenization); Chapter 2 (sampling) helps but is not required.
goals: Explain how Strata's serving layer divides the work: the HTTP service, the text front end, and an engine boundary with only one interface, generate
Rebuild a streamed answer in the right order: incremental UTF-8 decoding, cutting SSE events at blank lines, parsing complete JSON
Explain why tags and tool calls in the model's output must also be held and collected, and why model output is untrusted input

quiz.text: Is each chunk of bytes a client reads from the network always one complete SSE event?
choices: Always: the server writes one event at a time
Not necessarily: a chunk boundary can fall anywhere
Only Chinese gets cut apart, English does not
quiz.why: The network and the operating system decide the chunk size, so a chunk can end in the middle of a Chinese character, a piece of JSON or an event. English text gets cut too; it just never shows "half a character", because one English letter takes only 1 byte.

quiz.text: The UTF-8 encoding of the Chinese character 中 is E4 B8 AD. If a chunk of bytes ends with E4, what should a correct decoder do?
choices: Decode E4 as the replacement character � and read on
Hold E4 until the next chunk brings the 2 missing bytes
Drop E4, because it is not a whole character
quiz.why: E4 in binary is 1110 0100; the three leading 1s say the character has 3 bytes in all. When the chunk ends, 2 continuation bytes are still missing, so hold E4 and join it with the next chunk. Decode it as � or drop it, and the character is lost for good.

quiz.text: If you count the SSE events Strata sends back, do you know exactly how many tokens the model generated?
choices: Yes, one token per event
No, the two have no fixed relation
Only if there are no tool calls
quiz.why: The first event only announces that the assistant starts speaking; keep-alive comments appear while a long prompt is read; a token that brings only half a Chinese character has no text to send; and nothing may go out while a tag is held. To count tokens, read the usage field at the end.

problem: Each time a client receives a chunk of bytes, it decodes the chunk into a string, then parses every data line in it as JSON. Everything works in local testing, but users report that characters sometimes go missing and errors sometimes appear. Explain why, and give the correct order of processing.
answer: In local testing the whole answer often arrives in one or two chunks, so the problem stays hidden; on a slow network or behind a proxy the chunks get smaller and the boundaries fall in the middle of characters or events. Decoding each chunk on its own turns a split Chinese character into garbage; parsing an incomplete data line as JSON raises an error, and that event is lost. The correct order is three gates: first use an incremental UTF-8 decoder to join bytes into whole characters, holding incomplete bytes; then collect the text in a buffer and cut out a complete event only at a blank line, skipping comments that start with a colon; finally parse the complete data as JSON. How to test it: cut the same stream into chunks of every size from 1 to 32 bytes; the restored result must be exactly the same every time.

title: Lifecycle, cancellation and security boundaries
deck: "Stop answering" is a signal that has to cross the network, two processes and the GPU; authentication decides who may ask at all.
prereq: Chapter 23 (the serving layer and SSE); knowing the two phases from Chapter 1, prefill ("reading the prompt") and decode ("writing the answer").
goals: Draw the state machine of a request's lifecycle and explain why "cancelling" is a separate state
Explain how Strata cancels cooperatively: the watcher thread, the cancel flag, engine checkpoints, STOP, and draining to DONE
Explain what listening only on this computer by default, API keys and constant-time comparison each defend against

quiz.text: You click "Stop" on the web page and the text on screen freezes. Does that show the GPU has stopped computing for this request?
choices: Yes: once the page stops, the GPU stops
No: the cancel signal has to be passed down layer by layer and confirmed
Only for short answers
quiz.why: The web page is only the top layer. The server first has to notice the connection is gone and set the cancel flag, then write STOP to the engine; the engine still has to reach its next checkpoint, and the server releases the FIFO only after it reads this request's DONE.

quiz.text: Why does cancelling during prefill often take much longer than cancelling during decode?
choices: The network is slower during prefill
The engine checks only before each chunk starts, so it must finish the chunk in hand
The server does not check the cancel flag during prefill
quiz.why: During decode every token is a checkpoint, so it stops quickly. Prefill runs in chunks, and should_stop is checked once before each chunk starts; a chunk can hold up to 32768 tokens, and reading it can take well over ten seconds.

quiz.text: Strata compares API keys with hmac.compare_digest instead of an ordinary string equality check. What does this mainly defend against?
choices: Getting a wrong comparison result
An attacker guessing the key one character at a time by timing the comparison
Slow comparisons
quiz.why: An ordinary comparison returns at the first differing character, so the longer the correctly guessed prefix, the longer it takes, and that leaks information. A constant-time comparison always compares the whole string, so its time has nothing to do with how many characters were right.

problem: Write at least four checkable conditions for "cancellation complete", and explain why the wait for the engine to confirm it stopped must have a time limit.
answer: Conditions: ① once cancellation starts, no new token is committed to the client; ② the engine has stopped and written this request's own DONE (or was declared lost and its process ended); ③ this request's leftover output is not read by the next request, and its usage is not booked to another request; ④ the FIFO and other resources are released exactly once; ⑤ the client gets a clear "cancelled" or "failed" outcome, not "success". The wait must be time-limited because Strata holds the FIFO lock the whole time it waits for the STOP echo: if the engine is frozen, an unbounded wait leaves every later request queuing forever. When the limit is reached, the engine is declared lost and its process is ended, so the VRAM and RAM come back with the process, and the next request restarts the engine.

title: From one sequence to many users: a scheduler design class
deck: By default, upstream Strata serves one sequence at a time; since v0.1.39 you can turn on batch slots. This chapter is a design class: use scheduling algorithms and queueing theory to work out "how long the wait is", then see what must be isolated for multiple sequences.
prereq: Chapters 23 and 24 (the serving layer, the FIFO and the request lifecycle); expert routing from Chapter 10 and the KV cache from Chapter 17 help.
goals: Tell apart connections, queued requests, active sequences and sequences per computation, and explain upstream Strata's default FIFO, one-sequence behavior and the optional batch slots of v0.1.39
Compare FIFO, SJF and round-robin on waiting time and first-word time for the same requests, and use Little's law and M/M/1 to explain how utilization drives waiting
Explain the idea of continuous batching, and which state must be isolated and which budget must be reserved atomically before going multi-sequence

quiz.text: In the default setup, five people open the web page at the same time and ask the same upstream Strata a question. How many sequences are generating right now?
choices: Five: the HTTP server is multi-threaded
One: the other requests queue at the FIFO lock
It depends on how much VRAM the GPU has
quiz.why: The multi-threaded HTTP server lets all five connect, but there is a FIFO lock in front of the engine, and in the default setup upstream serves one sequence at a time. Connections and active sequences are two different numbers.

quiz.text: Three requests arrive together, with lengths 8, 3 and 5. Which policy gives the shortest average waiting time?
choices: FIFO, in order of arrival
SJF, shortest first
Round-robin with a time slice of 1
quiz.why: SJF runs them in the order 3, 5, 8, with waits of 0, 3 and 8, about 3.67 on average; FIFO averages about 6.33; round-robin lets everyone see a first word early, but its average wait is 7. The price of SJF is knowing the lengths in advance, and it may starve long requests.

quiz.text: Under the M/M/1 model, if a server's utilization rises from 80% to 95%, roughly how does the average time in the system change?
choices: A little longer, in proportion to utilization
It becomes 4 times as long
Almost no change
quiz.why: Average time in system W = service time ÷ (1 − ρ). At 80% it is 5 times the service time; at 95%, 20 times: exactly 4 times as long. The closer to full load, the more steeply waiting grows.

problem: You want Strata to serve two sequences at the same time. In the upstream code, the 36 GDN layers share one set of scratch space, the 12 QSA layers also share one set, and a comment says they "never run at the same time". Explain what this means for a multi-sequence rework, and write the test assertions for two requests arriving at the same moment for the last slot.
answer: The shared scratch space is correct only because of a hidden premise: "at any moment there is only one sequence, and layers run one after another". When two sequences really compute at the same time, the premise breaks: both sides write to the same scratch space at once, and their data get mixed into each other. A rework must dig out every such single-sequence assumption one by one: either scheduling guarantees the two sequences never use it at the same time (mutual exclusion), or each concurrent sequence gets its own scratch space, counted in the VRAM budget. Test assertions for the last slot: exactly one request gets a valid budget and becomes the active sequence, and the other queues or is clearly rejected; nothing is reserved twice, and a retry must not create two sessions; after completion or cancellation the budget is released exactly once; an old request must not write into the new slot's state.

title: Correctness testing: from one formula to a whole session
deck: Fluent text is the best liar. A test needs an independent reference answer, and it must first say what "equal" means.
prereq: Chapter 4 (floating-point numbers) and Chapter 10 (experts and top-k). Having read Chapters 18 and 20 makes the metamorphic-test examples easier to follow.
goals: Name the five layers of testing for an inference engine and the kind of bug each layer catches
Compare floating-point results with "relative tolerance + absolute tolerance", and judge when they must match bit for bit
Use differential tests and deliberately planted bugs to check whether a test really works

quiz.text: Two engines do floating-point additions in different orders, and the last few digits of their results differ. How should a test compare them?
choices: They must be bit-for-bit equal; any difference is a bug
Compare with a relative plus an absolute tolerance, and check separately whether the chosen word is the same
As long as neither side crashed, the test passes
quiz.why: Floating-point addition is not associative, so a different order changes the last few digits anyway, and a bit-for-bit comparison raises false alarms. But checking only "did not crash" tests nothing. A tolerance comparison lets legitimate order differences through; the chosen word can flip at near-ties, so record it separately.

quiz.text: A unit test checks "weighted sum" using only weight 1.0. Why can it not catch the bug "the weight is applied twice"?
choices: Because 1.0 squared is still 1.0, so the bug does not show on this input
Because unit tests cannot test addition
Because floating-point error hides the bug
quiz.why: Applying the weight twice turns w into w². At w = 1.0 the two are identical, so of course the test passes. Switch to uneven weights such as 0.7 and 0.3 and the result changes from 1.6 to 0.76, exposing the bug at once. A test with inputs that are too "tidy" is born blind to some kinds of bugs.

quiz.text: When comparing the expert cache on and off, why does Strata feed both sides the same reference text and compare position by position, instead of letting each side generate on its own and comparing afterwards?
choices: Because generating separately is too slow
Because after the first divergence the two sides have different context, so later positions cannot be compared
Because the reference text is shorter
quiz.why: In free generation, once a single word differs, the input to every later step changes, and the difference spreads all the way down. Teacher forcing shows both sides the same context at every position, so a divergence stays locked where it happened. Only then can you count "at how many positions the top word is the same".

problem: Strata's KV cache is stored in pages, and a page table locates each slot. Design a metamorphic test for "changing the paging scheme does not change the attention output", and explain how to confirm that the test really works.
answer: Build an uneven set of K/V values and a fixed query, and first compute a reference output with the simplest contiguous storage. Then store the same data with 1, 4 and 512 slots per page, shuffle the order of the physical pages at random while updating the page table, and compute attention. Require the selected logical slots and the output to match the reference. Since only the storage location changed and the order of operations did not, you can demand bit-for-bit equality (Strata's test demands exactly that). Finally, add a negative case: shuffle the physical pages without updating the page table, and the test must fail. If the negative case also passes, the test never actually read the page table.

title: Performance experiments: never move a number away from its conditions
deck: Run the same machine three times in a row and the speed can differ by almost a factor of two. A performance number needs its conditions, sample count and statistical method before it can stand up to questions.
prereq: Chapter 5 (bandwidth and throughput), Chapter 19 (speculative decoding), Chapter 25 (queueing and scheduling) and Chapter 26 (testing).
goals: Read the conditions behind a performance number and judge whether two numbers can be compared directly
Summarize a set of measurements with the median, percentiles and standard deviation, and explain why one outlier can drag the mean away
Design a measurement plan with warm-up, repetition and A/B alternation, and write down the formulas for TTFT and "speed"

quiz.text: Five requests take 8, 9, 10, 11 and 100 milliseconds. What is their median?
quiz.why: Sorted, the number right in the middle is 10. 27.6 is the mean, pulled up by that one 100-millisecond run; 100 is the maximum, which with fewer than 20 samples is also the p95 under the nearest-rank method.

quiz.text: To compare configurations A and B, you run A 3 times in a row, then B 3 times in a row. What is the most likely problem?
choices: No problem: the same number of runs is fair
All the slowness of a just-started machine falls on A, so B looks much faster than it really is
B is sure to slow down because the machine heats up
quiz.why: Caches, compute graphs and the file cache all need to "warm up", so the first few runs are usually slower. Finish A first and all that slowness lands on A. Warm up first, then alternate A and B, so changes in the machine's state are spread over both sides.

quiz.text: In the default setup, Strata's server handles one sequence at a time, and requests are served first come, first served. Five users send requests at once. Which metric gets worse first for the users who arrive later?
choices: Time to first token (TTFT)
The decode speed between tokens
The quality of the model's answers
